title: Asset Sale or Share Sale: The Structure Question That Changes What You Actually Walk Away With
linkedin:
Two businesses can sell for the exact same headline price and the owners walk away with completely different outcomes.

The reason is rarely the number on the term sheet. It's a decision usually raised by the buyer's lawyer a few weeks into the process: whether the sale is structured as an asset sale or a share sale.

A share sale transfers the whole legal entity, contracts and leases intact, but the buyer also inherits its history: old tax positions, old disputes, anything that hasn't surfaced yet.

An asset sale lets the buyer pick exactly what they're taking on and leave the rest behind. That's good risk management for the buyer. For the seller, it means every material contract and lease needs a landlord's, supplier's or regulator's sign off to move across, with no guarantee they all say yes on the same terms.

We see this tension turn up constantly in negotiations, usually disguised as a price conversation. A buyer proposing a lower price for a share sale to cover inherited risk. A longer settlement period requested for an asset sale so contracts can be reassigned before completion.

Structure and price are rarely decided independently of each other, even when they get discussed as if they were.

The owners who do best are the ones who understand which structure actually fits their business well before a buyer frames the conversation for them.

The reason usually isn't the price itself. It's a decision about how the sale is structured, an asset sale or a share sale, that often gets raised by the buyer's side a few weeks into the process rather than decided by the seller upfront.

A share sale transfers the whole company, including its history. An asset sale lets the buyer choose which assets and contracts to take on, which usually means every lease, supplier agreement and licence needs separate sign off to move across, and there's no guarantee everyone agrees on the same terms.

This single decision can change how smoothly a sale closes and what actually lands in the seller's account, well beyond the number on the term sheet.

For business owners thinking about a sale in the next few years, understanding this early, rather than reacting to whatever a buyer proposes first, puts you in a much stronger position.
